references.name: Aristotle
references.tldr: Greek philosopher who systematised logic, biology, physics and psychology. He treated the soul not as a ghost but as the organising principle of a living body, and described reasoning through syllogisms.
references.bach_take: Bach treats Aristotle as the origin of the scientific worldview and reads him as an animist in a modern, software-like sense. He also notes Aristotle's logic was only about 80% right.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: So in some sense, Aristotle is an animist.
our today's scientific worldview is very much, invented by Aristotle and goes back to him
Even Aristotle who thought about this very hard and came up with a theory of how syllogisms works
Bach says the notion of the feedback loop is already found in Aristotle.

references.name: De Anima (On the Soul)
references.author: Aristotle
references.tldr: Aristotle's treatise on the soul. It describes three levels: a vegetative soul (growth and nutrition, in plants), a sensitive soul (perception and desire, in animals) and a rational soul (in humans). The soul is the form of a living body and does not survive it.
references.bach_take: Bach uses it to argue that 'spirit' or 'psyche' originally meant a causal pattern that organises a body, which is what we now call software.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: And when Aristotle writes in De Anima about the spirit, the animus, the soul, the psyche, he does not envision our psyche, our soul, as something that is immortal
He basically said there are three levels of souls in nature, and he basically said that plants have the lowest one.

references.name: Prime mover (unmoved mover)
references.author: Aristotle
references.tldr: Aristotle's argument that since everything in motion is moved by something else, there must be a first cause of motion that is not itself moved. Medieval theology identified this first cause with God.
references.bach_take: Bach reads the prime mover as the automaton that runs the universe and calls equating it with a supernatural being a sleight of hand.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: the prime mover of Aristotle, which is basically the automaton that runs the universe
This idea to say that this prime mover is a supernatural being is complete nonsense.

references.name: Platonic forms
references.author: Plato
references.tldr: Plato's idea that the things we see are imperfect copies of ideal, abstract patterns (forms), such as the perfect circle or perfect justice.
references.bach_take: Bach borrows the term for ideal patterns that agents approximate: God as the Platonic form of a civilisation, and the soul as the ideal arrangement of a person's purposes.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: the natural shape of God is the platonic form of the civilization that you are part of
our true soul is the Platonic form, the ideal form of all these purposes arranged in the right hierarchy

references.name: Logos
references.author: Greek philosophy (Heraclitus, Stoics)
references.tldr: Greek term for the rational order or law that underlies the cosmos; later adopted by Stoics and by Christian theology ('In the beginning was the Word').
references.bach_take: Bach equates the Logos with the simplest self-existing mathematics from which the universe emerges, and links it to Wolfram's Ruliad.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: this pattern of the Ruliad is exactly the superposition of all the automata that is producing the universe, or the old Greeks called it Logos

references.name: Stoicism
references.author: Zeno of Citium and successors
references.tldr: A school of philosophy teaching that we suffer from our judgments about events rather than the events themselves, and that we should concern ourselves only with what is in our control.
references.bach_take: Bach finds its core advice obvious and asks why almost nobody follows it; his answer is that stoicism is probably maladaptive from an evolutionary perspective.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: I suspect that stoicism is maladaptive from a permanent evolutionary perspective
most cats I have known are stoics

references.note: The host introduces Stoicism; Bach picks it up.

references.name: Buddhism
references.author: Siddhartha Gautama
references.tldr: A contemplative tradition that studies experience from the inside through meditation, teaching that the self is constructed and that suffering comes from attachment. Advanced practitioners report being able to deconstruct ordinary perception and selfhood.
references.bach_take: Bach credits Buddhist meditators with reaching the 'enlightenment' stage in which one sees how experience is constructed, but says Buddhism is limited to the inside perspective and is not interested in physics. In 2018 he was dismissive of its Western form and its metaphysics.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Buddhism to me is limited to this inside perspective
You most basically find this mostly with advanced Buddhist meditators and so on
I got to know Buddhism only in its um westernized forms
Bach compares the Catholic view of the mundane world to what Eastern philosophers call samsara.

references.name: Jainism
references.tldr: An Indian religion built around radical non-violence (ahimsa): harming any living creature should be avoided.
references.bach_take: Mentioned alongside Buddhism as a tradition that extends care to the suffering of other creatures once you identify with other agents.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Buddhism and so on and Jainism the idea that suffering of other creatures should be avoided

references.name: Dalai Lama (reincarnating office)
references.author: Tibetan Buddhism
references.tldr: In Tibetan Buddhism the Dalai Lama is held to be reborn in each generation; a child is identified as the successor and trained into the role.
references.bach_take: Bach's illustration that identity is a construct: the Dalai Lama identifies not as a human being but as a form of government that runs on successive humans.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: He's basically a governmental software that is instantiated in every new generation
To kill the Dalai Lama, you have to kill his tradition.

references.name: Genesis 1 (creation story)
references.author: Hebrew Bible
references.tldr: The opening chapter of the Bible: a spirit hovers over formless waters, separates light from darkness and heaven from earth, makes plants, animals and finally humans in its own image.
references.bach_take: Bach reads it not as the creation of the physical universe but as a description of how a mind boots up: consciousness creating a world model and then a self inside it. He and co-author Hikari Sorensen wrote their own version in a paper.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: I suspect that it’s there in plain sight in Genesis 1, in this first book of the Bible
I think that Genesis is actually the childhood memories of a God.
the entities that are being described in genesis are not entities of physics
Host: Bach and Hikari Sorensen 'wrote their own Genesis' in their paper (page 20), which he reads aloud.

references.name: Adam and Eve / Garden of Eden
references.author: Hebrew Bible
references.tldr: The biblical story of the first humans living in a paradise without suffering until they eat from the tree of knowledge and are expelled.
references.bach_take: Bach says there are several non-literal readings that make sense; one is that Eden describes a phase of life (being happily in love) rather than a historical place.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: there was no garden of eden that we ever lived in in which all the animals were vegetarians and there was no suffering

references.name: Tower of Babel
references.author: Hebrew Bible
references.tldr: Biblical story in which humanity builds a tower to reach heaven until God confuses their languages so the builders can no longer understand each other.
references.bach_take: For Bach it is a founding myth about the collective project of understanding the universe (a metaphysical building, philosophy and science), and a metaphor for parts of a mind losing a shared protocol.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: it's a metaphysical building that is being built
not get subject to some kind of Tower of Babel

references.name: The Bible
references.year: c. 8th c. BCE to 2nd c. CE
references.tldr: The canonical scripture of Judaism and Christianity, a library of myths, laws, histories and poetry.
references.bach_take: Bach read it as a child to understand the canon of his society and thinks it contains real philosophical insights hidden by a simplistic literal interpretation.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: I forced myself through the Bible
the bible has a number of very interesting philosophical insights in it

references.name: Catholicism / the Catholic Church
references.tldr: The largest Christian church, which organised European society for over a thousand years around shared doctrine, ritual and a notion of the sacred.
references.bach_take: Bach describes it as an operating system for society: software installed on minds to synchronise people into a larger agent ('God'), at the cost of damaging their epistemology and obscuring the study of mind.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: the Catholics used a relatively crude methodology to implement software on the minds of people
the Catholic civilization is one that obfuscated the area of the mind, because, it made it all part of a mythology
Bach says Catholics burned down and later imperfectly rebuilt the Greek and Roman 'cathedral' of understanding, leaving scars in our epistemology.

references.name: Protestantism
references.author: Martin Luther and others
references.tldr: The branch of Christianity that emerged from the Reformation, stressing the individual's direct relationship to God and personal conscience.
references.bach_take: Bach says most atheists he knows are 'super Protestants' who still serve a sacred greater whole, and he calls Miyazaki the most relevant Protestant philosopher today.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: most atheists that I know are actually super Protestants
makes Miyazaki into the most relevant Protestant philosopher today

references.name: Thomas Aquinas
references.tldr: Medieval Catholic philosopher who merged Aristotle with Christian theology in the Summa Theologiae.
references.bach_take: Bach re-read Aquinas as a rational designer of an 'operating system' for Catholic society, not a dualist, and asks how his rules for cooperating agents could apply to AI alignment.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: a philosopher who thought deeply about this was Thomas Aquinas, foremost philosopher of Catholicism
I recently re-read Thomas O'Kynes.
starting out with re-reading and reconsidering aquinas

references.note: lex101 auto-transcript renders Aquinas as 'Thomas O'Kynes'; context (Aristotle, Catholic society, virtues) makes the resolution clear.

references.name: Seven virtues (four cardinal, three theological)
references.author: Thomas Aquinas (after Plato, Aristotle, St Paul)
references.tldr: The classical list of prudence, justice, temperance and courage, plus the Christian faith, hope and love.
references.bach_take: Bach decodes them as policies for agents that must cooperate: temperance is internal regulation, justice is regulation between agents, prudence is picking the right goals, courage is acting on your models; faith, hope and love are commitments to a shared higher-level agent. He proposes love (shared purpose) as an answer to AI alignment.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: they are additionally 02:30:57 to these four cardinal virtues, three divine virtues
you should optimize your internal regulation, which he calls temperance
The commitment to shared purpose is the core of love.

references.name: Animism
references.tldr: The widespread belief that living things (and sometimes places and objects) are inhabited by spirits that make them act.
references.bach_take: Bach argues animism is close to the truth if 'spirit' is read as self-organising agentic software; spirits need not be supernatural.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: All cultures outside of ours are animist cultures
The spirit doesn't have to be supernatural.
it’s an old word that just means operating system for an autonomous robot

references.name: God as a collective agent
references.author: Joscha Bach (reinterpreting monotheism)
references.tldr: The proposal that 'God' names the agent that emerges when many individuals coordinate around a shared highest purpose, the way cells form an organism.
references.bach_take: This is Bach's own secular reading of religion: gods are selves that span many minds, and the single God is the global optimum of collective agency.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: the global optimum of collectively enacted agency has a name. We call this God.
It's basically the super organism that is formed by the individuals as an intentional agent.

references.name: Golem
references.author: Jewish folklore
references.tldr: A creature of clay brought to life by inscribed words, which carries out instructions literally and without judgment.
references.bach_take: Bach's image for language models and paperclip maximisers: machines that execute a task with nobody home. In 2026 he also describes chips as sand etched by 'alchemists' on which golem-like minds emerge.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: My intuition is that the language models that we are building are golems.
there are minds emerging on them that are like golems, and we can talk to them

references.name: Qigong
references.author: Chinese contemplative practice
references.tldr: A Chinese system of breathing, movement and attention exercises said to cultivate 'qi' energy.
references.bach_take: Used as an example of reported telepathy-like abilities that Bach thinks might be explained by rethinking neuroscience rather than physics.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: if you talk to a Qigong practitioner in China who is cultivating his key energy

references.name: René Descartes and the Meditations
references.tldr: French philosopher famous for 'I think, therefore I am' and for dividing reality into extended stuff (res extensa) and thinking stuff (res cogitans), the classic statement of mind-body dualism.
references.bach_take: Bach suspects Descartes was smarter than his reputation and wrote some religious arguments under political pressure. He reinterprets the two substances as two kinds of mental representation: the spatial world model and the realm of ideas.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: he is often smarter than people give him credit for
So res extensa is the thing, that for instance, Jeff Hawkins at Numenta, is so obsessed with.
Bach maps Genesis's two worlds onto res extensa and res cogitans (captioned as 'res extensor and dress cognitions').

references.name: Occasionalism
references.author: Malebranche and other Cartesians
references.tldr: A post-Cartesian doctrine that mind and body never directly interact; God causes the matching events on each side on every occasion.
references.bach_take: Bach cites it as evidence that the generation after Descartes simplified his thinking when trying to explain how a causally closed physical world could interact with a mental one.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: that is especially apparent when you look at Occasionalism

references.name: Leibniz's mill
references.author: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (Monadology)
references.tldr: A thought experiment: enlarge a thinking machine to the size of a mill and walk inside; you will see only parts pushing each other and nothing that explains perception.
references.bach_take: Bach says the intuition fails because it looks at the wrong level: mind is a causal pattern (software) over the parts, not the parts themselves. It is the title theme of his 2026 MLST interview.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: leibniz says this idea of imagine you could have a Mill and this this is your mind
What is a causal pattern? Right? We call it software.

references.name: Julien Offray de La Mettrie (Man a Machine)
references.tldr: French physician-philosopher who argued that humans are machines and that mental life arises from bodily mechanisms.
references.bach_take: Cited as an early appearance of the feedback-loop idea: competing springs in the mind that keep it in dynamic balance.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: we find it in La Mettrie, where he describes that, there must be systems of competing springs in the mind

references.name: German Romanticism
references.tldr: A literary and artistic movement that prized nature, feeling, longing and the individual imagination, partly in reaction to Enlightenment rationalism.
references.bach_take: Bach names the literature of Romanticism and German poetry as a formative influence, and says he grew up in a region of Thuringia shaped by it.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: the classical philosophers and also the literature of romanticism
it's an area of German Romanticism which had a pretty big influence on how I grew up

references.note: lex101 lists authors as 'Druster Hildeshoff andainer and Up to Hesse'; the first is almost certainly Annette von Droste-Hülshoff, the second is unresolved (possibly Heine or Eichendorff). Hermann Hesse is named, but it is unclear whether by Bach or the host.

references.name: Undine and The Little Mermaid
references.author: Friedrich de la Motte Fouqué; Hans Christian Andersen
references.tldr: Two versions of the water-spirit tale. In the older Undine story the water woman kills the unfaithful prince with a kiss; in Andersen's version the mermaid gives up her voice and finally her life for love.
references.bach_take: Bach tells both to his children instead of the Disney version, and uses them to say the mermaid is right: you sacrifice for romantic love. He also uses 'sirens eat people' as a parable about loving something that does not share your purposes.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: And I think that the mermaid is right. You sacrifice your life for romantic love.
The Little Mermaid is a siren Sirens eat people

references.note: 'Anderson' in the transcript is Hans Christian Andersen; 'Undin' is Undine.

references.name: Oscar Wilde
references.tldr: Irish writer of plays, fairy tales and aphorisms, associated with aestheticism and tragic romantic stories.
references.bach_take: Bach says reading Wilde early 'inoculated' him with romanticism.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: I read Oscar Wilde before I read the other things

references.name: Heidi
references.author: Johanna Spyri
references.tldr: Swiss children's novel about an innocent orphan girl in the Alps whose goodness transforms the people around her.
references.bach_take: Bach reads Heidi as an embodiment of European Protestantism: a pure being committed to serving God whom civilisation exists to protect.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Heidi is an embodiment of this spirit of European Protestantism

references.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
references.tldr: German philosopher who attacked conventional morality and religion and announced the 'death of God'.
references.bach_take: Bach is irreverent: Nietzsche is smart and readable but took himself too seriously and ended in tragedy.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: I think that Nietzsche is the classical equivalent of a shit poster.

references.name: Karl Marx on capitalism's crises
references.author: Karl Marx
references.tldr: Marx argued that capitalism is inherently unstable: its own dynamics produce recurring crises even as it creates enormous productivity.
references.bach_take: Bach agrees with this diagnosis (capitalism is divergent, not convergent) while rejecting communism and anarchism as solutions.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: I think that Marx was correct in saying that capitalism is prone to crisis.

references.name: Charles Darwin as 'the last philosopher'
references.author: Charles Darwin (remark attributed to Mikhail Gromov)
references.tldr: Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection explained the design of living things without a designer.
references.bach_take: Bach relays a remark by the mathematician Misha Gromov that Darwin was the last person able to connect the dots in a completely fresh way; Bach himself thinks some philosophy is still being done, mostly in the foundations of mathematics.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Misha gromov once told me he's a mathematician that in his perspective Darin was the last philosopher

references.note: Auto-caption says 'Darin'; resolved to Darwin from context with moderate confidence.

references.name: Jürgen Habermas and dialectical materialism
references.tldr: Habermas is the leading post-war West German social philosopher; dialectical materialism was the official Marxist philosophy of East Germany.
references.bach_take: Bach's point is that after the Nazi era both Germanies lost their rigorous philosophical tradition.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Western Germany didn't get much more edgy than Habermass

references.name: Cantor's set theory and its paradoxes
references.author: Georg Cantor
references.tldr: Cantor built mathematics on sets and showed there are different sizes of infinity. Naive set theory then produced paradoxes such as a total set that must contain all of its own subsets.
references.bach_take: Bach's starting point for why infinities break mathematics: the contradictions show classical mathematics cannot be run without 'crashing'.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Hilbert stumbled on counter set theoretic uh experiments to deal with natural numbers
Hilbert saw that, for instance, a country's sets here where the experiments and mathematics led into contradictions.

references.note: 'counter set theoretic' and 'a country's sets here' are auto-caption manglings of 'Cantor's set-theoretic' / 'Cantor's set theory'.

references.name: Hilbert's program
references.author: David Hilbert
references.tldr: Hilbert's call to put all of mathematics on a secure footing by finding a complete, consistent set of axioms and mechanical rules of proof.
references.bach_take: For Bach this was the bug report that led Gödel and Turing to discover that only the computable part of mathematics works.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: All these issues led Hilbert to saying, please mathematicians, there seems to be something wrong here.
which is in some sense what Grydol and Turing discovered in response to Hilbert's call

references.name: Principia Mathematica
references.author: Bertrand Russell and Alfred North Whitehead
references.tldr: A monumental attempt to derive all of mathematics from logic, using a hierarchy of types to block self-referential paradoxes.
references.bach_take: Bach says their restriction was too strong (we do think in loops) and that Gödel showed the attempt was insufficient anyway.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Russell and Whitehead and Principia Mathematica were attempting to do this by limiting set theory

references.name: Peano axioms
references.author: Giuseppe Peano
references.tldr: A handful of axioms that define the natural numbers and arithmetic from zero and a successor operation.
references.bach_take: Bach uses them to explain Gödel's method (arithmetic emulating logic) and notes that even 'zero' needs a number system, so non-existence is not a free default.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: He basically built an emulator using Peano arithmetic to express a logical language.
Bach: once you have Peano's axioms (captioned 'pianos axioms') you have a Turing-complete system from which a universe could be built.

references.name: Gödel's incompleteness theorems
references.author: Kurt Gödel
references.tldr: Gödel showed that any consistent formal system rich enough for arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove, by making the system talk about itself.
references.bach_take: Bach's distinctive reading: Gödel did not find a limit of computation but a bug in classical, stateless mathematics with infinities. The fix is to use only constructive (computable) mathematics. He stresses that Gödel himself, a Platonist, was shocked by the result.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: And what Gödel has discovered is that these bugs cannot be eliminated except by redefining the programming language of mathematics.
And what Gödel has shown in my view is that constructive mathematics is real
It basically 16:02 shook his world to the core
girdle was a true realist that is he thought that truth really exists out there

references.note: Gödel appears as 'Gurdl' (lex101), 'Grydol' (lex212), 'girdle'/'Guru' (mlst82).

references.name: Constructive mathematics and intuitionism
references.author: L. E. J. Brouwer and later constructivists
references.tldr: A school of mathematics that accepts an object only if you can give a procedure to construct it, rejecting proofs that merely assert existence and treating infinity as a never-finished process.
references.bach_take: Central to Bach's worldview: constructive mathematics is 'the part of maths that works' and is the same thing as computation. Computationalism is a form of constructivism, and physics borrowed non-constructive mathematics before this was understood.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: constructive mathematics is the part of maths that works and it happens to be the same as computation
And constructive mathematics is roughly the same thing as computation.
I think in classical mathematics, the first formulation was Intuitionism.

references.note: Brouwer is not named in the transcripts; the 2026 transcript says 'I don't think that he formulated it very well' without a clear name.

references.name: Alan Turing and the Turing machine
references.tldr: Turing defined computation with an abstract machine that reads and writes symbols on a tape, and showed that one universal machine can run any program.
references.bach_take: For Bach, Turing understood what Gödel did not: mathematics was computation all along. He also holds that minds are in the class of universal computers, with finite resources.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: I think that Turing could see that the solution is to understand that the question mathematics was computation all along
as long as brains are Turing complete, you can build minds on different substrates

references.name: Church–Turing thesis
references.author: Alonzo Church and Alan Turing
references.tldr: The claim that every reasonable model of computation can compute the same things, so any computer can emulate any other given enough time and memory.
references.bach_take: Bach's main weapon against substrate-based theories of consciousness, especially IIT: an emulation produces the same reports, so consciousness cannot depend on the physical layout.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: It's the insight that every computer can emulate every other computer.
So, in some sense IIT is not compatible with the Church-Turing thesis

references.name: Computing Machinery and Intelligence (the Turing test)
references.author: Alan Turing
references.tldr: Turing proposed replacing 'can machines think?' with an imitation game: if a machine's conversation cannot be told apart from a human's, treat it as intelligent. The paper also discusses objections, including one from telepathy.
references.bach_take: Bach notes that Turing took telepathy seriously, and that the Turing test is about performance and so cannot test for consciousness. A true test would be an AI that explains how AI works.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Turing’s famous 1950 paper in which he describes the Turing test, he does speculate about telepathy
Turing's test does not care about how you produce the dialogue
I think that a true Turing test would require that an AGI explains how AGI works.

references.name: Lambda calculus, Lisp and rewrite systems
references.author: Alonzo Church; John McCarthy
references.tldr: A way of defining computation as repeated search-and-replace on expressions rather than a machine stepping along a tape. Lisp is the programming language built on it.
references.bach_take: Bach has come to see rewrite systems as the most general view of computation, with the Turing machine as a special deterministic case; a branching rewrite system gives a multiverse.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: The Turing machine is a very special case of a rewrite system.
the Lambda calculus and the turing machine turn out to have the same power

references.name: Ludwig Wittgenstein
references.tldr: Austrian philosopher. His early work tried to define exactly what can be said in a logical language; his later work argued that meaning comes from how language is used in life.
references.bach_take: Bach says Wittgenstein pre-empted the logicist program of AI by decades and anticipated Turing's universality (logic from NAND gates). He sides with the late Wittgenstein: language is not fundamental to cognition, and images/perception were the unsolved part.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Wittgenstein basically preempted the logitist program of AI that Minskie started 17:09 later
I agree with Wittgenstein. I just agree with the late Wittgenstein.
Turing was actually a pupil of Wittgenstein.

references.note: 'non-calculus'/'non-gates' in the transcript are NAND; 'Vidkins stands' is Wittgenstein.

references.name: Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus
references.author: Ludwig Wittgenstein
references.tldr: A short, numbered treatise that tries to state the limits of what can be meaningfully said by treating language as a logical picture of facts.
references.bach_take: Bach calls it probably the most beautiful philosophical text of the 20th century: an attempt to turn philosophy into a logical programming language.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: I think that the track titles itself is probably the most beautiful philosophical text that was written in the 20th century.

references.note: Auto-transcript renders Tractatus as 'attractados', 'tractatos' and 'track titles'.

references.name: Philosophical Investigations
references.author: Ludwig Wittgenstein
references.tldr: Wittgenstein's late work, which abandons the idea of one logical language and looks at meaning as use in 'language games'.
